feedback.solution: A systematic pattern means the model is wrong for the data; a straight line through a curve misestimates unknowns.

options: The response is curved over this range; use a narrower range or a non-linear fit.
The fit is excellent because the residuals average to zero.
One standard was pipetted wrongly and should be deleted.
The blank was wrong but the curve can be used.

questions.prompt: Why make a new standard curve for each run of an assay?

feedback.hint: What could differ between today and last week?
feedback.solution: Standards and samples must be measured under the same conditions; reagents age and instruments drift.

options: Reagent activity, standards and instrument response change between runs, so an old curve may not describe today's measurements.

It is required only for fluorescence assays.

questions.prompt: Which statements about absorbance measurements are correct? Select all that apply.

feedback.hint: Consider the definition of absorbance, stray light, and the limits of the calibrated range.
feedback.solution: A = 2 is T = 0.01; stray light limits high readings; values below the curve are not quantified. The law fails at high concentration, and plate path length depends on the liquid depth.

questions.prompt: pH buffers read +0.8 mV at pH 7.00 and +166.9 mV at pH 4.01 at 25 °C. What is the slope as a percentage of the theoretical 59.16 mV per pH unit? Give %. Keep full precision in intermediate calculations. Enter the number only, to three significant figures.

feedback.hint: Slope = ΔmV/ΔpH; divide by 59.16.
feedback.solution: (166.9 − 0.8)/2.99 = 55.55 mV per pH; 93.9% of theoretical, so the calibration fails a 95–105% limit.
